faqs.q: What tech stack do you use?
faqs.a: I'm stack-agnostic — I pick what fits the project. React/Next.js for web, React Native or Flutter for mobile, Electron/Tauri for desktop. Backend: Node.js, Laravel, or Python depending on needs. No religious wars here.
Fixed-price after scope is defined. Most projects land between $800–$5,000 depending on complexity. No surprise hourly bills — the number in the proposal is the number you pay.

faqs.q: How long does a project take?
faqs.a: Simple apps: 2–3 weeks. Medium complexity: 4–6 weeks. Full platforms: 6–8+ weeks. I'll give you a timeline before we start and flag risks early.

faqs.q: Do you work with clients remotely?
faqs.a: Yes — I'm based in Batangas, Philippines (GMT+8) and have worked with clients across timezones. Async-first communication, with calls scheduled when needed.

faqs.q: Can you maintain the app after launch?
faqs.a: Yes. I offer post-launch support, feature additions, and maintenance packages. Most clients stay on a monthly retainer for ongoing work.

posts.title: Building an offline-first POS system with Tauri
posts.excerpt: How I built a desktop POS app that works without internet, syncs data when connected, and fits in a 5MB installer.

p: Most POS systems die when the WiFi does. My client needed something that works in a sari-sari store with spotty internet — and it needed to be fast, not a bloated Electron wrapper.

Tauri uses the system's webview instead of bundling Chromium. The result: a 5MB installer instead of 150MB, and memory usage that doesn't make old laptops cry. Rust backend means the core logic is fast and safe.
SQLite for local storage, CRDTs for conflict resolution, and a sync layer that queues changes when offline and pushes them when the connection returns. No data loss, ever.

A desktop POS that boots in under a second, handles transactions offline, and syncs inventory to the cloud every time it connects. The client said it feels like 'cheating compared to the old system.' That's the best compliment.

posts.title: React Native: one codebase, two platforms, real performance
posts.excerpt: Why I chose React Native for a client app, and how I made it feel native on both iOS and Android.

p: The 'just use native' crowd has valid points. But when your budget covers one team and two platforms, React Native is the pragmatic choice — if you know where the leaks are.

Most React Native performance issues come from re-renders, not the bridge. Memoize aggressively, flatten your lists, and use Reanimated for anything that moves. The 60fps is there if you respect the rules.
Platform-specific code is fine. iOS gets a bottom sheet, Android gets a drawer. Users don't know they're running the same JS bundle — they just know it feels right.
One codebase, 95% shared, both apps shipped to stores in under 8 weeks. The client's feedback: 'I can't tell which one is the native app.' Mission accomplished.

posts.title: Why Next.js is my default for full-stack web projects
posts.excerpt: Server components, API routes, and the deployment pipeline that makes shipping feel effortless.

p: Next.js isn't perfect, but it removed 80% of the decisions I used to spend time on. File-based routing, server components by default, and Vercel deployment means I ship faster.
Data fetching at the component level, zero client JS for static content, and automatic code splitting. The mental model is simpler than any SPA framework I've used.
When you don't need a separate backend server, Next.js API routes handle auth, webhooks, and small data endpoints perfectly. One deploy, one codebase, done.
Highly dynamic real-time apps, complex background processing, or when you need a specific backend framework. Not everything needs to be a full-stack React framework.

posts.title: From pixel-pusher to full-stack: my journey into code
posts.excerpt: How I went from Figma files to React components, and why the transition made me a better developer.

p: I got tired of handing off designs and hoping developers would build what I imagined. So I learned to build it myself. The first app was terrible. The third one was usable. By the fifth, clients were asking for code, not mockups.

Understanding visual hierarchy, spacing, and color theory means I ship UIs that don't need a designer review. I can implement Figma files pixel-perfect because I think in both design and code simultaneously.

blocks.h: What I wish I knew earlier
p: Code is just problem-solving with syntax. The hardest part isn't the language — it's deciding what to build. Start with the problem, not the technology.
